{
  "body": "The three problems you describe are connected: you disagree about what agreements meant because they were vague; the vague agreements keep breaking because your schedules change; and your friend is avoiding the conversations because, from their side, they probably feel fruitless or accusatory. So treat this as one problem about how you make agreements, not three separate fights about chores.

First, talk to the avoiding friend alone, before any group meeting, and not about any specific chore. Ask what the conversations are like for them and listen without defending yourself. Their avoidance is information: perhaps the talks happen at bad times, run too long, or feel like blame sessions. You will not fix the format until you know which it is.

Second, propose changing the process rather than relitigating past failures. Suggest one short, scheduled house meeting, thirty minutes at most, with the stated aim of changing how you agree, not deciding who was right last month.

Third, make every agreement concrete and written. A shared note or a kitchen whiteboard listing each task, who owns it this period, when it is due, and what counts as done. Most of your later disputes come from 'clean the kitchen' meaning three different things, and from honest memory differences about who said what. A definition of done and a written record remove most of both.

Fourth, build in flexibility. A rigid weekly rota will keep generating unfairness as shifts change. Instead hold a ten-minute weekly reset to allocate the coming week's tasks around actual schedules, and allow swaps. If one person's schedule is chronically worse, consider compensating contributions: they buy the supplies, take the less visible tasks, or chip in for an occasional cleaner.

Fifth, negotiate the standard explicitly once. Many chore arguments are really standard arguments, and that is a legitimate thing to disagree about and compromise on.

Finally, keep the whole system light. If maintaining it becomes a chore of its own, it will collapse. And accept that you only control your side: even if your friend will not re-engage, you can still stop relitigating, be specific in your own commitments, and acknowledge your part in the pattern.",
  "commitments": "Taking this up involves several concrete acts and exposures. It commits you to a low-pressure one-to-one with the avoiding friend before calling any group meeting, and to listening there without rebutting; raising it as an ambush about chores would confirm whatever made the conversations feel bad in the first place. It commits you to proposing a written, specific agreement format and to accepting the small ongoing overhead of maintaining it, with the stated risk that the upkeep itself becomes a new chore and quite possibly yours. It commits you to a weekly reallocation in which you will sometimes accept the worse share, and to stating and negotiating your own minimum cleanliness standard rather than treating it as obvious.

The advice depends on the assumption that the disputes are mainly ambiguity-and-logistics problems. If the friend's withdrawal reflects a deeper grievance, such as a long-standing sense that effort is uneven or that the deck is stacked, a process fix alone will not hold; the one-to-one is partly a test of which situation you are in.

Open criticism to keep in view: the written record can be attacked as bureaucratic or as a device for winning arguments rather than ending them. Its defence is that it targets exactly the failure you reported, namely disagreement about what was agreed; deployed pointedly or triumphantly it will instead deepen the avoidance.

Unresolved: whether the friend will re-engage at all; whether three different standards can actually be reconciled; and how any system survives a genuinely chaotic week, which is when it will first be tested."
}

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?
